Dear Medical Director / Utilization Review Committee,

I am writing to formally appeal the denial of prior authorization for catheter ablation for atrial fibrillation (AF) for my patient. This procedure is medically necessary and is supported by the 2023 ACC/AHA/ACCP/HRS Guideline for Diagnosis and Management of Atrial Fibrillation, multiple randomized controlled trials, and CMS coverage policy NCD 20.8.3.

This patient has [PAROXYSMAL / PERSISTENT] atrial fibrillation, first diagnosed {{letter_date}}, with [DESCRIBE SYMPTOMS: palpitations, dyspnea, fatigue, exercise intolerance, presyncope]. Symptoms have significantly impacted quality of life, limiting [DESCRIBE FUNCTIONAL IMPACT].

ANTIARRHYTHMIC DRUG HISTORY:
The patient has failed the following antiarrhythmic drug therapy:
• [DRUG 1]: [DOSE], [DURATION] — failed due to [INEFFICACY / INTOLERANCE: describe]
• [DRUG 2 if applicable]: [DOSE], [DURATION] — failed due to [INEFFICACY / INTOLERANCE: describe]

This satisfies the requirement for failed AAD therapy prior to catheter ablation per the 2023 ACC/AHA/ACCP/HRS Guidelines (Class I recommendation after AAD failure).

EVIDENCE-BASED JUSTIFICATION:

1. 2023 ACC/AHA GUIDELINE SUPPORT:
Per the 2023 ACC/AHA/ACCP/HRS Guideline for Diagnosis and Management of Atrial Fibrillation (Joglar JA, et al., J Am Coll Cardiol 2024;83:109-279):
• Catheter ablation is a Class I recommendation for patients with symptomatic paroxysmal or persistent AF who have failed or are intolerant of ≥1 Class I or III antiarrhythmic drug
• Catheter ablation is a Class IIa recommendation as first-line therapy for symptomatic paroxysmal AF
• Pulmonary vein isolation (PVI) is the cornerstone of AF ablation with success rates of 70–85% for paroxysmal AF

2. RANDOMIZED CONTROLLED TRIAL EVIDENCE:
The CABANA trial (Packer DL, et al., JAMA 2019;321:1261-1274) demonstrated that catheter ablation significantly reduced AF recurrence and improved quality of life compared to medical therapy. Per-protocol analysis showed significant reductions in the composite endpoint of death, disabling stroke, serious bleeding, and cardiac arrest.

[IF HF PRESENT]: The CASTLE-AF trial (Marrouche NF, et al., NEJM 2018;378:417-427) demonstrated that catheter ablation in patients with AF and heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) significantly reduced all-cause mortality (hazard ratio 0.53, p=0.01) and hospitalization for worsening heart failure compared to medical therapy.

3. PRE-PROCEDURE EVALUATION:
• Transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) / CT angiography: [RESULT — no LAA thrombus confirmed]
• Anticoagulation: [DESCRIBE — therapeutic DOAC/warfarin for ≥3 weeks pre-procedure]
• Electrophysiology consultation: {{letter_date}} — rhythm control strategy recommended

4. RISK OF DENIAL:
Without catheter ablation, this patient will continue to experience [DESCRIBE: symptom burden, AF recurrence, quality-of-life impairment, risk of AF-related complications including stroke, cardiomyopathy, hospitalization]. Continued antiarrhythmic drug therapy has been unsuccessful and poses ongoing risks of [DESCRIBE AAD SIDE EFFECTS].
